claims.text: The untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and fracture strain of 13.5%.
A controlled aging treatment near 700 °C for several hours can precipitate nanoscale HfC or a similar refractory carbide in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The aging treatment will produce a high-density, homogeneous distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Low-temperature aging can suppress precipitate coarsening and retain a fine precipitate size.
Nanoscale HfC particles act as strong dislocation-pinning sites.
Precipitation strengthening will enhance strain hardening in dynamically loaded HfZrTiTa0.53.
The precipitates will redistribute plastic strain and generate additional back stresses.
Precipitation-induced strain hardening and back stress will reduce local strain localization.
The aged alloy will exhibit a higher dynamic yield strength than the untreated alloy.
The aged alloy will exhibit improved uniform plastic deformation and a higher dynamic fracture strain.
The aged alloy will delay the initiation and propagation of adiabatic shear bands.
Delayed shear localization will reduce the rate of catastrophic dynamic failure.
The intervention will modulate impact-induced energy release.
The prediction applies to split-Hopkinson-pressure-bar loading at strain rates around 10^3 s^-1 under substantially adiabatic conditions.
Thermal softening and shear localization are prominent under the specified dynamic conditions.
Extreme strain rates or aging outside the optimal window may diminish the beneficial effects.
Hat-shaped split-Hopkinson-pressure-bar specimens can be used to compare dynamic shear localization in untreated and aged samples.

The hypothesis is falsified if the aged samples show no statistically significant improvement in dynamic strength, uniform deformability, and shear-band suppression relative to matched untreated controls.
